vignette:
A 50-year-old South Asian woman, a career diplomat currently posted at her country's embassy in Geneva, came to see me after several years of feeling "stuck." She is single, lives alone, and has always prided herself on composure and precision. But in the past few years, she has found it increasingly hard to hold herself together.

The traumatic event happened seven years ago, when she was serving as a deputy chief of mission in a conflict-affected country. During a routine inspection of a humanitarian aid warehouse, a pressurized cylinder of industrial chlorine gas malfunctioned and released a cloud of yellow-green vapor. She was only a few meters away. For a few seconds she could not breathe; her eyes burned and her throat closed. Colleagues dragged her outside, but not before she inhaled enough to cause chemical pneumonitis. She was hospitalized for two days, then evacuated to a neutral country for follow-up. Physically she recovered fully, but something changed.

In the months afterward, back in her home capital, she began to avoid anything that reminded her of that day. She stopped going to the gym because the smell of bleach in the locker room made her heart race. She threw away her favorite silk scarf-the one she had been wearing that morning-because it still faintly carried a trace of chemical odor. At work, she found herself struggling in meetings when anyone mentioned "chlorine" or "water treatment." She would suddenly feel a tightness in her chest, a surge of heat, and the need to leave the room. She made excuses: allergies, a headache, an urgent phone call.

Her occupation demands that she remain calm under pressure, maintain diplomatic language, and project unshakable poise. She has always been excellent at this. But now, even the smallest triggers-a whiff of cleaning fluid in the embassy hallway, a news article about industrial accidents, the beep of a smoke detector-can send her into a spiral. She has learned to control her outward reactions, but inside she feels like a tightly wound spring. After one such incident during a high-level negotiation, she excused herself to the restroom and spent five minutes staring at her own reflection, breathing deliberately, counting backward from ten. No one noticed, but she felt ashamed.

Her personal life has narrowed. She used to enjoy cooking complex South Asian dishes, but now she avoids most strong spices and especially any recipe that requires bleach or ammonia for cleaning. She has stopped accepting dinner invitations at restaurants with open kitchens, worried that the smell of propane or sanitizer might trigger an intrusive memory. She has not told any of her colleagues about the incident; she fears being seen as weak or "damaged." Her parents live abroad and she speaks to them weekly, but she always reports that she is fine.

At night, she often wakes at 3 a.m. with the sensation of not being able to breathe. She lies still, hands on her chest, waiting for the feeling to pass. When she does sleep, she dreams of the yellow-green cloud and the panicked shouting. She has stopped drinking tea in the evenings because even the steam reminds her of the inhalation.

In our sessions, she speaks of her work with a mixture of pride and dread. She still performs well, but she is always watching the door, always scanning for exits. Recently, she was assigned to negotiate a multilateral treaty on chemical safety-a file directly related to her trauma. She did not request reassignment. She says she should be able to handle it. But the thought of reading those documents makes her skin crawl. She has started delaying her work, letting paperwork pile up, which is unlike her.

She is here because she finally realized that she cannot will herself out of this. Her PCL-5 score of 34 confirms what she already knows: the event is still present, alive inside her, even though the physical scars healed years ago. She wants to stop being afraid of the air itself. But she is not sure if she can be both a diplomat and a person who sometimes has to step out of a room to survive her own memories.
